newsitem.title: UK: Chelsea Football Club's Harding dies in air crash.
newsitem.headline: Chelsea Football Club's Harding dies in air crash.

text.p: Matthew Harding, multi-millionaire vice-chairman of Prime Minister John Major's favourite football team Chelsea, was killed in a helicopter crash on Tuesday night, the club said on Wednesday.
Harding, 42, was one of five men who died when the helicopter crashed in a field on the way back to London after a match between Chelsea and Bolton Wanderers in northwest England.
Earlier this year, Harding hit the headlines when he gave one million pounds ($1.60 million) to the opposition Labour Party, the biggest donation by an individual in the party's 90-year history.
"It is confirmed that Matthew C. Harding...was killed last night," the company that owns Chelsea football club said.
The other crash victims had not been named by midday.
The Eurocopter Twin Squirrel came down at about 11.00 pm (2200 gmt) on Tuesday evening in Cheshire, northwest England.
Residents heard a helicopter engine in difficulties and then saw it explode in flames as it hit the ground. Police ruled out the possibility of a mid-air collision.
They first suspected Harding was among those killed when they found a charred football programme among the wreckage.
Harding, Britain's 89th richest man, began his working life as an office junior. By his early 40s he was chairman of one of Britain's most profitable reinsurance companies, Benfield Group.
Although Chelsea's most prominent supporters include Major and former Conservative cabinet minister David Mellor, Harding was a supporter of the left-leaning Labour Party.
Labour leader Tony Blair described Harding's death as "an appalling tragedy."
"We all feel devastated for his family. He was so full of life and vigour and someone deeply committed to his country," Blair said.
Major offered "heartfelt condolences to his family and to the families of all who died in this terrible accident".
Despite his great wealth and jet-set lifestyle, Harding endeared himself to Chelsea fans with his down-to-earth ways.
On match days, he would enjoy a beer in the Imperial Arms, a pub near Chelsea's Stamford Bridge ground.
He chatted happily with fans about football and he watched matches from the public stand rather than the directors' box.
"He was a real football fan. Even a major business coup didn't give him the same thrill as Chelsea scoring," said Mellor, now a part-time sports broadcaster.
Tearful football fans delivered flowers to the gates of Stamford Bridge after hearing the news.
"You did Chelsea Proud," read the message from one fan.

Among tributes faxed to news organisations was one from Richard Branson, the British multi-millionaire who heads the Virgin group of companies and whose failed attempt to fly round the world in a balloon last year was part-financed by Harding.
"We will all miss him and our hearts go out to his family," Branson said.
Last year, Harding was involved in a public feud with Chelsea chairman Ken Bates year over control of the club, but the dispute was finally resolved amicably.
"Our hearts and thoughts go out to the people who surround Matthew and his fellow unfortunate passengers in the crash," Bates said.

Harding bought Stamford Bridge for 16.5 million pounds ($26 million) in 1995 and provided more cash for stadium improvements and to buy top overseas players including Italians Gianluca Vialli and Roberto Di Matteo and France's Franck Leboeuf.
Harding was married with four sons.
